text: Long ago, there were no fridges. So in eighteen thirty three, a ship carried a mountain of ice all the way from America to Calcutta. The trip took four months. And more than half of the ice was still ice when it arrived! <#0.3#> So how does a fridge keep your food cold? Let's find out. <#0.3#> First, try this. Wet your hand, and blow on it. Feels cold, right? When water dries up, it takes heat away with it. That is the whole secret of a fridge. <#0.3#> In seventeen fifty five, a teacher in Scotland, William Cullen, made ice just by letting a liquid dry up really fast. In eighteen thirty four, Jacob Perkins patented a machine that did this again and again, in a loop. That's the grandfather of your fridge. <#0.3#> Inside your fridge, a special liquid runs through thin pipes. It dries up into a gas, and grabs the heat from your food. Then a pump squeezes the gas. Squeezing makes it hot. At the back, the hot gas gives its heat to your room, and turns back into liquid. Round and round it goes. <#0.3#> Here's the funny part. A fridge doesn't make cold. It carries heat out of the box, like a bucket carrying water out of a boat. That's why the back of your fridge feels warm! Even Albert Einstein helped invent a fridge. The nineteen thirty patent had no squeezing pump at all. <#0.3#> In India, Godrej says it made the first Indian fridge in nineteen fifty eight. Today, about thirty eight out of every hundred homes have one. <#0.3#> Now you know.
